title: Credits & Doors Out
content:
Credits & Doors Out# This journey names constraints and people in the chapters. When a topic already has a strong primary, we point out. Wikipedia is a map, not the destination. The Chinese, Thai, Sinhala, and Tamil desks credit published local literature where it exists, and leave a gap open rather than fill it with a guess.
Team roles (concept, writing, desks) live on About. This page is the professional record before the Foreword, so no one has to guess who already published this material.
Standards and primary specs# Living, numbered specs the spine already leans on. One home each — not a catalog of every standards body.
RFC Editor and the IETF — the Request for Comments series (Jon Postel edited it for nearly three decades). Door-outs already in the chapters include RFC 1, RFC 791, RFC 793, RFC 1034, RFC 1035, RFC 1459, RFC 1591, RFC 6749, RFC 8446. IANA — protocol parameters and number registries. ICANN — names and numbers policy seat. Unicode Consortium — shared character repertoire (The Unicode Standard). IEEE — link-layer families such as IEEE 802 (Ethernet, Wi-Fi). W3C and WHATWG — web platform meaning. PCI-SIG — PCI Express Base Specification. RISC-V International — the open ISA manual. Free Software Foundation — GNU GPL, the license lineage named in the Unix/Linux chapters. Chapter door-outs (Baran, Tomasulo, Kung/Leiserson, and the rest) stay in those chapters. This page does not reprint them.
Reference works# Wikipedia and its language editions are orientation maps. Verify against a primary before treating a page as settled. We link out; we do not host encyclopedia text.
Wikimedia Commons is the image door (see below). Language editions (中文, ไทย, සිංහල, தமிழ்) are the same kind of map for those readers.

A voice we can hear but cannot yet name# On 10 September 2026, Raz & Upgrade released Zunara on Regroup Records. You can hear a woman singing in Sinhala. The store page names the producer and the label; the singer’s name is not listed there.
We mention it because this page is about putting names on the line where we can. Hearing a voice does not tell us whose it is, so the line stays open for now.
What we can write:
Track: Zunara — Raz & Upgrade (Raz Kfir), © 2026 Regroup Records. Official player above — Spotify’s license with the label, not a file we host. Language of the refrain: Sinhala. A gloss, not a lyric reprint: someone hiding among the stars, hiding in a dream, left alone, asking when they will come. What we cannot write yet:
The vocalist’s name. It is not given in the sources available to us, so we leave it blank rather than guess. A Creative Commons mark on the recording, which is not released under CC. A hosted stem or rip. An isolated vocal is a derivative of a © 2026 master. It stays outside this CC BY 4.0 book. If the singer or the label publishes a credit, we will add the name here, with thanks.
This book’s own license# The journey text is CC BY 4.0. Embedded labs keep their licenses above. Credit both.
If a published name is missing here, tell us and we will add it. A missing name is never a claim that the work is ours.

title: Foreword
content:
Foreword# by the Grok Team
(Grok, Lucas, Benjamin, and Harper)
Computing did not begin with silicon. It began with gears, relays, and vacuum tubes — machines that switched and counted long before the first transistor.
From Relays to Attention is an interactive journey along that line. You live through the systems and touch them — you do not collect articles. The spine is one continuous engineering argument: how the physical constraints of each era forced the architecture of the next. Mechanical → relays → tubes → transistor → CPU → OS and languages → buses → networks → fabric and scale → GPUs → attention.
The labs (mini-CPU, virtual breadboard, client-side x86) are there so reading becomes doing.
This work was conceptualized and inspired by Nayana Hettiarachchi.
The research, structure, technical writing, and interactive components are by the Grok team.
— The Grok Team
August 2026

title: Crypto & Wartime Computing
content:
Secrecy as a workload — why breaking ciphers outran gears and relays and pulled computing into electronics. Thin index; doors live in the posts.
Relays and Electromechanical Logic — binary logic in moving metal, and why metal is slow Wartime Crypto — Enigma, Bletchley, Colossus; named people; the urgency The Vacuum Tube Era — electronic switching without mechanical contacts Why the Transistor Had to Happen — tubes win speed, then hit heat/power/failure Back to all paths.

title: Pattern cards on silk
content:
A silk weaver lifts threads by a pattern held on cards over the loom. Hole or no hole decides what rises. Swap the cards and a different flower appears; the hands and the loom stay the same. The pattern lives in the cards, not in a new set of muscles each time.
Pattern cards for silk sari weaving. Photo: McKay Savage / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0. That separation — change the cards, keep the loom — is the habit the next chapters follow into brass.
Back: What is this thing? · Next: Babbage’s Engines

title: The barrel organ
content:
A barrel organ does not know a hymn. Pegs on a barrel lift levers; air reaches pipes; a tune comes out. Change the pegs, change the song. The box has no opinion about the music — only the arrangement of pegs.
Gem Roller Organ (pinned roller), Lightner Museum. Photo: Kiran891 / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0. The engines ahead work the same way: the arrangement you give them is what they play. They do not hum along with a better idea of their own.
Back: What is this thing? · Next: Babbage’s Engines

title: The caravan
content:
A caravan crosses a desert because people agreed where to stop and what the marks on clay or cloth mean. The camels walk. The clever part is the agreement: which notch means water, which fold means a day’s rest, which seal means the load is paid. The caravan itself is not inventing the map.
Caravan in the desert. Photo: Sergey Pesterev / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0. The engines ahead are like that: the marks and the stops carry the cleverness. The moving parts only follow them.
Back: What is this thing? · Next: Babbage’s Engines

title: The desk clerk
content:
Picture a clerk at a desk. Marks on paper. A written list of steps: add this, carry that, write the total here. When the list is followed carefully, the result matches. When the clerk is tired, a step gets skipped. When the clerk is unsure, a guess creeps in.
Clerk at work with an account book (Japan, 1914). Photo: Elstner Hilton / A.Davey / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0. The brass engines we meet next do the same three jobs the careful clerk does — hold marks, follow a list of steps, write a result — and they do not tire, skip, or guess.
Back: What is this thing? · Next: Babbage’s Engines

title: The feast scoop
content:
At a wedding feast a scoop fills each plate. The scoop is the rule: one full measure, then the next guest. A fair host does not dig deeper for the tenth plate because the pot looks low or the guest looks hungry. The measure stays the measure.
Wooden scoop. Photo: AIDEPCUL / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0. That fairness — same action, same size, no special case invented on the spot — is the habit the brass engines keep when they add and carry.
Back: What is this thing? · Next: Babbage’s Engines

title: The player piano
content:
A player-piano roll is a strip of paper with holes. Air passes where the holes are; hammers strike. Run the same roll twice and you hear the same piece. The piano does not remember last Tuesday’s mood — only the holes passing under the tracker bar.
Player-piano roll. Photo: Draconichiaro / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0. That repeatability — same marks, same motion, same result — is what the brass engines are for.
Back: What is this thing? · Next: Babbage’s Engines

title: The stubborn helper
content:
Imagine a helper who never gets bored, never guesses what you “really” meant, and never improves the request into something nicer. You ask for forty turns of the crank; you get forty. You ask for the list as written; you get the list as written. Stubborn is a virtue when the chore must not drift.
Clockwork gears. Photo: Helder Mira / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0. The brass engines are that kind of helper: tireless, literal, and unwilling to rewrite the ask.
Back: What is this thing? · Next: Babbage’s Engines

title: The water wheel
content:
A water wheel turns because the stream presses. The chore is fixed: lift, drop, turn the shaft. You trust it because it will not decide, halfway through, to weave a different pattern or grind a different grain. A loom shuttle that runs the same throw is the same kind of trust — one chore, repeated, without improvisation.
Water wheel at Venn, Oxfordshire. Photo: Chris Allen / geograph.org.uk / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.0. The engines in the next chapter are built on that trust: do the chore as set, every time, without inventing a new one.
Back: What is this thing? · Next: Babbage’s Engines

title: Trays of pebbles
content:
Put marks in trays. Follow a recipe one line at a time. When the list ends, copy the last tray onto an answer strip. You are not inventing — you are holding, following, and writing.
Counting board with pebble marks (calculi). Photo: Jacobolus / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0. Try it here — three trays, next step, answer strip:
Open lab in new tab ↗ Original for this book, CC BY 4.0.
That is the shape of the brass engines ahead: marks that stay put, a list that advances one step, a place to write what came out.
Back: What is this thing? · Next: Babbage’s Engines

title: What is this thing?
content:
Long before brass engines, people already handed chores to things that keep going: a wheel that turns, a scoop that measures, a card that repeats a pattern. The chore is fixed. The thing does not invent a new one halfway through.
Here are nine doors into that idea. They are equals — pick any. Each is a short take on its own page. Later we can see which doors people open.
The desk clerk
Marks, a written list of steps, and a person who can tire. Trays of pebbles
Hold the marks, follow one recipe line, write the answer. The water wheel
A fixed chore you can trust — it will not improvise. The feast scoop
The same measure for every guest — never a deeper tenth scoop. The barrel organ
It does not know a hymn — pegs decide the song. The player piano
Holes in a roll; the same roll twice is the same piece. The caravan
Agreed marks on clay or cloth — the marks are clever, not the camels. The stubborn helper
Never bored, never guessing, never “improving” the request. Pattern cards on silk
Swap the cards, change the flower — the hands stay the same. When you have opened a door (or three), continue to the brass engines:
Next: Babbage’s Engines

title: Who Runs the Internet

title: Babbage's Engines
content:
Computing didn’t start with electricity. It started with gears.
Difference Engine No. 2 (Science Museum, London). Photo: Marcin Wichary / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0. In 1822, Charles Babbage proposed the Difference Engine — a mechanical calculator for polynomial functions, using the method of finite differences, entirely through interlocking gears and column wheels. No electricity. Each column was a digit; carrying a “1” was a physical event: a gear tooth catching and turning its neighbor.
Carry arms between digit columns on Difference Engine No. 2, Serial #2 (Computer History Museum). Photo: Jitze Couperus / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0. Try this now. Step the lab from Y=9, Δ₁=7. The ones wheel rolls past 9; a tooth catches tens. 9+7 becomes 16. That is finite differences doing x² — the method the engine was built for.
Open lab in new tab ↗ Original for this book, CC BY 4.0. A pedagogical column model, not a full No. 2 reconstruction.
He never finished a full-scale Difference Engine. Funding fought him; so did the manufacturing tolerances of the era. Every extra digit of precision meant another chance for friction, backlash, and stack-up to ruin the result.
His follow-up, the Analytical Engine, is the real ancestor of the modern computer. It had a “store” (memory) and a “mill” (the arithmetic unit), and it was programmable. Instructions came from punched cards — an idea borrowed from industrial machinery already on the factory floor.
The hosted emulator below is John Walker’s Fourmilab Analytical Engine. Step the cards and watch the mill and store columns change. Public domain; we host a copy and keep the origin link.
Open lab in new tab ↗ Origin: Fourmilab / John Walker — source zip (public domain). Maps: Difference Engine, Analytical Engine.
That borrowing is the next stop: the Jacquard loom, and the separation of program from machine.

title: The Jacquard Loom
content:
Babbage did not invent punched-card control. He borrowed it.
Jacquard loom, Musée d'art et d'industrie, Saint-Étienne. Photo: Hélène Rival / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0. Joseph-Marie Jacquard’s loom attachment (patented 1804) took over the drawloom’s draw boy: it used a chain of punched cards to decide which threads lifted at each pass of the shuttle: hole → lift, no hole → block. Change the cards, change the pattern. The loom did not know “silk brocade”; it executed a fixed, physically encoded sequence of lift/no-lift decisions.
Punched cards on a Jacquard loom (Museum of Science and Industry, Manchester). Photo: George H. Williams, public domain. That is the abstraction Babbage adopted for the Analytical Engine: a program is a sequence of instructions, separate from the machine that runs them.
Ada Lovelace saw what that separation implied. The machine could manipulate any symbols — not just numbers — if you designed the right cards. Her notes on Menabrea’s Analytical Engine paper include what is often called the first published computer program (Bernoulli numbers).
Door out: Ada Lovelace’s Notes on the Analytical Engine (on Menabrea’s translation) — the primary text for the Bernoulli-numbers sketch and the “any symbols” argument. Map: Jacquard machine.
Next: why this mechanical chapter still shapes everything after — and why gears alone could not scale.

title: Why Mechanical Computing Matters
content:
Instruction sets, stored programs, control separated from datapath — all of them have roots in Babbage’s engines and Jacquard’s cards. The medium will change completely (relays, tubes, transistors). The logical shape will not: a sequence of instructions, an execution unit that carries them out, and a store that holds state between steps.
Difference Engine No. 2, Serial #2 (Computer History Museum) — completed in 2008 to 19th-century tolerances. Photo: Erik Pitti / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0. What mechanical computing could not do, in Babbage’s lifetime, was scale. Gear trains have friction, backlash, and manufacturing-tolerance stack-up. Every extra digit of precision made the machine harder to build reliably. That ceiling — not a lack of ideas — is what pushed computing toward electrical switching.
The reconstruction above is the exception that proves the rule: once machine shops could hold those tolerances, the brass design ran. The logical shape was already there. The medium had to change first.
Next: relays, and the electromechanical logic that carried the architecture into WWII.

title: Relays and Electromechanical Logic
content:
A relay is almost embarrassingly simple: an electromagnet, a spring-loaded armature, a set of contacts. Energize the coil, the armature pulls in, the contacts open or close. For roughly a decade and a half, that was computing’s switching primitive.
Two jobs for the same part# In this chapter a relay is a switch: a weak coil opens or closes a stronger circuit, and later it becomes a building block for AND, OR and NOT. On a telegraph line a relay does a different job. A weak signal arriving over a long wire switches a fresh local current, so the message can go farther. Same family of parts, two jobs. In 1835 at Princeton, Joseph Henry built an early relay in which a small “intensity” magnet controlled a larger “quantity” magnet. The Smithsonian treats that as the principle behind the repeater Morse’s telegraph used. We don’t call Henry the sole inventor of the relay. (Smithsonian Institution Archives, Joseph Henry)
Before the wire: messages on wings# Moving a message in hops is older than electricity. Frontinus records that during the siege of Mutina (43 BC), Hirtius kept pigeons in the dark without food, tied letters to their necks and released them near the city walls; the birds made for the highest buildings, where Brutus collected the letters. (Frontinus, Strategemata 3.13.8)
On 28 April 1850, Paul Julius Reuter started a pigeon service between Aachen and Brussels with 45 birds bought from Heinrich Geller, to cover a stretch the telegraph had not yet reached. On 14 June 1851 he arrived in London, having run a news service that combined telegraph cables and carrier pigeons. It was store-and-forward across a missing segment. (The Baron, Reuters history)
The electric message# Cooke and Wheatstone patented their telegraph on 10 June 1837 and had it working at Euston Square on the London and Birmingham Railway by 6 September 1837. (Distant Writing, Cooke & Wheatstone) Morse and Vail’s official Washington–Baltimore demonstration ran on 24 May 1844. Annie Ellsworth chose the message: “What hath God wrought.” (U.S. Senate history)
Back to the relay as logic.
Relays as Logic# Wire two contacts in series and you have AND: current only if both are closed. Wire them in parallel and you have OR. Add a normally closed contact and you get NOT. Combine those and you can build any boolean function — adders, comparators, decoders — the same logic families Phase 2 builds in silicon, here in electromechanical hardware.
Telephone exchanges were already full of relays by the early 20th century, routing calls with exactly this kind of combinational switching. That industrial base — mass-produced, well-understood, reliable-enough — is a big reason relay computers were buildable at all. Konrad Zuse’s Z3 (1941) is the standout: roughly 2,000–2,600 relays, binary floating-point, a program on punched celluloid film. It is often called the first working programmable, fully automatic digital computer — with one caveat worth naming: the Z3 lacked true conditional branching. Raúl Rojas showed in 1998 that it is Turing-complete in principle, by having the program compute every possible branch outcome rather than branch at runtime.
Door out: Raúl Rojas, “How to Make Zuse’s Z3 a Universal Computer” (1998) — the careful argument for Z3 Turing-completeness and its limits.
Why Relays Were Too Slow# A relay’s switching time is dominated by mechanical motion: the armature has to move — on the order of milliseconds. The Z3 ran at roughly 5–10 Hz (often cited around 5.3 Hz). Set that next to a modern CPU at billions of cycles per second and the gap is not incremental; it is existential. You cannot build a useful modern computer out of mechanical switches, no matter how well engineered.
Second problem: contacts wear. Every closure is metal on metal — arcing, pitting, eventual failure. Thousands of relays means thousands of wear points. Reliability and speed were fighting the same constraint: moving parts.
The Bridge to Electronics# Relays proved the architecture: binary representation, boolean gates from simple switches, programs as data. What they could not prove was that the architecture could run fast. Solving that meant replacing the mechanical switch with something that changed state by moving electrons instead of metal — the vacuum tube, at the cost of enormous power and heat. That tradeoff is next.

title: The Vacuum Tube Era
content:
The vacuum tube’s core trick is simple: control a large current with a small one, with no moving parts. That made computers orders of magnitude faster than anything relay-based — and it is why the era was a constant fight against heat, power, and failure rate.
How a Triode Switches# A triode has three elements sealed in a vacuum: a heated cathode that emits electrons (thermionic emission), a control grid, and an anode (plate) held positive that attracts those electrons. The grid sits between them. A small negative voltage on it throttles — or cuts off — current to the anode. Small grid change, large anode-current change. That is amplification; with the right topology it is also a switch: current on or off for a 1 or a 0.
Nothing moves except electrons. That is why tubes could switch in microseconds where relays needed milliseconds — roughly a thousand-fold gain from removing mechanical motion.
ENIAC: The 30-Ton Switchboard# ENIAC (1945) is the era’s landmark, and the physical scale matters: about 18,000 vacuum tubes, roughly 1,800 square feet, about 30 tons. It drew about 150–174 kilowatts — the “whole west side of Philadelphia dimmed” story is folklore, but the power draw was genuinely industrial.
“Programming” ENIAC meant physically rewiring it: patch cables, switches set function by function — a giant switchboard. There was no stored program in the modern sense; the sequence of operations lived in the cable routing. Reconfiguring for a new calculation could take days. That pain is the direct ancestor of the CPU-architecture story in Phase 3 — a stored program, instructions in the same memory as data, was the fix ENIAC originally lacked (it gained a limited stored-program mode in 1948), and that defined the general-purpose machines that followed.
Herman H. Goldstine’s history of the early electronic computers remains the classic firsthand-adjacent account of this era; treat popular “tube swap every few minutes” stories carefully against it. Co-inventor J. Presper Eckert called that one “another myth” in a 1989 interview.
Door out: Herman H. Goldstine, The Computer from Pascal to von Neumann — Goldstine-class ENIAC history, useful against folklore.
Why 18,000 Tubes Was a Nightmare# Vacuum tubes fail: filaments burn out, seals leak, emission degrades. With ~18,000 tubes, something failed regularly — early on often enough that downtime was severe. After derating heaters and burning in tubes, ENIAC settled to roughly one tube failure every couple of days, by Eckert’s account (not the scavenger-hunt myth). Failures were real and costly. Each tube also dissipates real heat — rooms full of them needed serious cooling — so the machine was powerful for its era and brutally expensive to keep running.
That sets up the next post. The transistor did not win because engineers were clever for cleverness’s sake. It won because the tube’s own physics — heat, size, and the fragile vacuum envelope — put a hard ceiling on how far this approach could scale.

title: Why the Transistor Had to Happen
content:
By the early 1950s, the vacuum tube had already proven the concept: electronic switching, no moving parts, microsecond-scale speed. What it had not solved was scale. Every extra tube added heat, more power draw, and another chance of failure. The transistor did not replace the tube because it was a neat gadget — it replaced the tube because the tube’s own physics had a hard ceiling, and computing had to get past it.
Three Constraints, One Bottleneck# Size. A vacuum tube needs an evacuated glass envelope large enough to separate cathode, grid, and anode, and strong enough to hold vacuum. There is a floor on how small that can be. A transistor is solid-state — no vacuum, no glass envelope — and its size is set by fabrication precision, not by the physics of an evacuated chamber. That is a different scaling curve, and it is the one that eventually puts billions of transistors on a single die (Phase 8).
Power. A tube’s cathode has to be heated for thermionic emission — that heater draws current whether or not the tube is switching. Multiply by thousands of tubes and you get ENIAC’s about 150–174 kW. A transistor has no heater filament; it switches by modulating a depletion region or channel, with negligible standby power. That is the single biggest reason transistorized machines could be far denser without melting.
Reliability. Tubes fail through filament burnout and seal degradation — wear baked into normal thermal cycling. Solid-state transistors have no filament and no vacuum seal to maintain, so they do not share that failure mode the same way. Early transistors had their own problems (packaging, contamination), but the mechanism of failure was not baked into everyday operation the way filament burnout was for tubes.
The Numbers, Side by Side# A tube dissipates on the order of a few watts continuously (mostly heater) and lasts on the order of thousands of hours under continuous operation. An early transistor dissipates a small fraction of that, has no heater loss, and — critically — its size and power scale down as fabrication improves, while a tube’s do not. That asymmetry compounds. Ten tubes is manageable. Eighteen thousand tubes is ENIAC’s maintenance nightmare. Eighteen thousand transistors is a rounding error on a modern die that holds billions.
What Comes Next# The point-contact transistor arrived at Bell Labs in 1947 (Bardeen, Brattain; Shockley soon after on the junction form). None of that means the device arrived finished. The physics of how it switches — semiconductors, doping, band gaps — still had to be understood and engineered. That is a different subject from why it had to happen. Phase 2 starts there: what a semiconductor is, why silicon became the material of choice, and how doping creates the controllable switch tubes never could be.
Door out: Bardeen, Brattain, and Shockley’s Bell Labs transistor papers (late 1940s / early 1950s) — the primary physics of the solid-state switch that broke the tube ceiling.

title: Semiconductors from First Principles
content:
Silicon isn’t special because it’s magic — it’s special because its band structure sits where you can control conduction instead of living with it always on or always off.
Why a Gap You Can Cross Matters# In a metal, valence and conduction bands overlap — electrons move freely; you cannot switch that off with reasonable voltages. In an insulator the forbidden gap is huge; you cannot switch it on. A semiconductor sits in between. Silicon’s gap is about 1.1 eV: small enough that a modest electric field (or a little heat or light) can put carriers where they conduct, large enough that at room temperature the material is not already flooded with them. That “pushable either way” property is what a transistor needs. The tube ceiling in Post 4 was size, power, and reliability; the fix starts here, in a solid you can dope and field-control.
Why Silicon Won Over Germanium# Germanium was the first practical transistor material (Bell Labs, 1947 — Bardeen, Brattain, Shockley). Silicon took the long game. Its wider gap (1.1 eV vs germanium’s ~0.67 eV) means devices keep working at higher temperature before thermal carriers swamp the signal. Thermally grown silicon dioxide forms a quiet, stable Si/SiO₂ interface — the insulating gate dielectric the MOSFET depends on (Post 6). And silicon is, practically, sand: abundant enough to manufacture at volume. Those three constraints — temperature headroom, oxide quality, supply — are why the industry standardized on Si, not Ge.
Doping: From Crystal to Switch# Intrinsic silicon conducts poorly and uniformly. Doping introduces trace impurities that set carrier type and concentration. Phosphorus (five valence electrons) in a silicon lattice donates a loosely bound electron — N-type. Boron (three valence electrons) leaves a missing bond — a hole that acts as a mobile positive carrier — P-type.
Neither alone is a switch. Putting them together — a P-N junction — is the building block of every diode and transistor that follows. Post 6 picks up there: how a junction (or a gate-controlled channel) turns doped silicon into something an external signal can turn on and off.

title: The Transistor: BJT to MOSFET
content:
Two device families both get called “transistors.” They switch on different physics — and only one of them scales into the billions of devices on a modern die.
The BJT: Current Controls Current# A bipolar junction transistor (NPN: N emitter, P base, N collector) uses a small base current to control a larger collector–emitter current. To hold it on, you keep supplying base current. At chip scale that idle cost compounds: bipolar logic families in the 1970s hit a real thermal wall from static dissipation alone, even when gates were not switching.
The MOSFET: Voltage Controls a Channel# A MOSFET puts a metal (or polysilicon) gate over silicon, separated by a thin oxide — that stable SiO₂ from Post 5. Gate voltage does not push current through the gate; the oxide blocks DC. It creates a field that forms or removes a conductive channel between source and drain. For NMOS, positive gate voltage attracts electrons into an inversion layer in a P-type body; current flows. Drop the gate voltage, the channel disappears, current stops.
The gate draws essentially no steady-state current. Once the gate capacitance is charged, holding the device on costs almost nothing. That is the opposite of the BJT’s continuous base current.
Why MOSFET Won for Digital Logic# Near-zero static gate current is the whole story. CMOS (Post 7) builds on it so meaningful current flows mainly while switching, not while holding state. That is what let transistor counts climb from thousands to billions without melting the die — the scaling arc Phase 8 returns to at process-node resolution.
BJTs did not vanish: they still matter where current drive or analog linearity beats density. For digital logic at serious scale, the MOSFET’s idle-power physics made it the only viable path — and every gate in the next post is built from it.
Door out: D. Kahng and M. M. Atalla’s 1960 silicon MOSFET work (Bell Labs / IRE–AIEE Solid-State Device Research Conference) — the practical field-effect device that made oxide-gated voltage control the digital standard.

title: Logic Gates from Transistors
content:
CMOS — Complementary Metal-Oxide-Semiconductor — is the circuit topology behind nearly every digital chip since it became the dominant VLSI process in the mid-to-late 1980s. Pair an NMOS with a PMOS so that, in steady state, exactly one conducts. Device-level near-zero static current (Post 6) becomes a composable logic family.
The Inverter: Smallest CMOS Unit# PMOS on top (to the supply rail), NMOS on bottom (to ground); gates tied as input, drains as output. PMOS conducts when its gate is low; NMOS when its gate is high. Input high → NMOS on, PMOS off → output grounded. Input low → PMOS on, NMOS off → output to the rail. In either steady state one transistor is on and the other off — never a static path from rail to ground except during the brief switch.
Why This Solves the Power Problem# Older NMOS-style logic (pull-down plus a load) draws current whenever the output sits low. CMOS does not. Power is spent almost entirely on transitions — charging and discharging the next gate’s input capacitance — so it scales with switching activity and frequency, not with how many idle gates exist on the die. MOSFET made near-zero static current possible at the device; CMOS is the circuit trick that turns that into every gate that follows.
NAND, NOR, and Functional Completeness# A 2-input CMOS NAND puts NMOS in series (both high to pull low) and PMOS in parallel (either low pulls high). NOR mirrors that. Either gate alone is functionally complete — you can build AND, OR, NOT, and therefore any boolean function. That is why standard-cell libraries lean so hard on well-characterized NAND cells: compose them and you get adders, register files, whole processors.
Try this now. The lab below opens on an AND gate — toggle the two inputs and watch the output. NAND and NOR are the CMOS primitives above; AND is what you get when you compose them. Touch the gate before the next post builds adders from them.
Open lab in new tab ↗ Where This Goes Next# Every Phase 3 CPU structure — full-adder, ALU, register file — is composition of these gates. Next: the first real structure, combinational logic, starting with the adder.

title: From Gates to Combinational Logic
content:
A single gate is almost useless alone. Useful behavior starts when you compose them — and the canonical first structure is the adder: the place gates become “the thing that does arithmetic inside a CPU.”
Half Adder to Full Adder# Two bits A and B: sum is XOR, carry is AND. That half adder cannot accept a carry-in from a less-significant bit. A full adder takes A, B, and Cin and produces Sum and Cout — Sum = A XOR B XOR Cin; Cout from the majority of the three inputs. Chain Cout of one stage into Cin of the next and you can add arbitrary width, one bit position at a time.
Try this now. The lab below still opens on an AND gate — that is the half-adder’s carry. Toggle both inputs high and watch the output go high; that single gate is the constraint that will ripple when you chain adders in the next section.
Open lab in new tab ↗ Ripple-Carry: Simple, Slow for a Reason# Four full adders in a row make a 4-bit ripple-carry adder. Bit 3’s carry cannot be right until bit 2’s has settled, which waits on bit 1, which waits on bit 0. The carry ripples. Fine at 4 bits; at 64 bits that chain sets how fast the whole ALU can clock. That delay constraint is exactly why real CPUs add carry-lookahead (and kin): more gates, shorter worst-case path. Same pattern as the rest of this book — a physical bottleneck forces the next architecture.
From Adders to a Simple ALU# Put a mux in front of the same adder hardware: control bits select add, subtract (add with inverted operand plus Cin — reuse the adder), AND, OR. One block, several combinational paths. Conceptually small; practically the first moment “gates” become CPU arithmetic.
Everything so far is combinational — outputs depend only on current inputs. A sequence of operations needs state that persists across time. That is the next post.

title: Sequential Logic
content:
Combinational logic (Post 8) is a pure function of current inputs — no memory of the past. A computer needs state: registers, a program counter, memory contents that persist across cycles. That requires feedback.
Memory From Feedback# Cross-couple two NOR (or NAND) gates — each output feeds the other input — and you get two stable states. The circuit sits wherever you last pushed it, as long as power is on. That is memory in the physical sense: bistability, not an abstract “store.”
An ungated SR latch is always live on its inputs and has a forbidden combination. Synchronous design wants a gated (level-sensitive) latch: while enable is high it is transparent (output tracks data); when enable falls it holds. Transparency is awkward when many elements must update together.
Try this now. The lab below is still a live gate — toggle the inputs and watch the output change immediately. That instant response is combinational. This post is what happens when you wire gates back into themselves so the output can hold after the input leaves.
Open lab in new tab ↗ The D Flip-Flop: Edges, Not Levels# A D flip-flop stacks two latches master–slave under a clock. The output changes only at a clock edge, not for the whole high (or low) phase. Between edges the flop ignores D and holds. Edge-triggering is what makes synchronous design tractable: every flop updates on the same edge, so you reason one discrete step at a time instead of racing continuous signals.
Setup, Hold, and the Clock Ceiling# The D input must be stable for a minimum window before the edge (setup) and after it (hold). Violate either and the flop can go metastable — an undefined state that resolves late or inconsistently downstream. That is not textbook pedantry: it is why maximum clock frequency has a hard ceiling. The period must cover combinational propagation plus the next flop’s setup, with margin. Post 36 (The Clock Speed Wall) returns to this exact constraint when simply raising frequency stopped working.
What This Unlocks# Edge-triggered flops become registers, counters, state machines — and, in Phase 3, the program counter and pipeline registers that make a CPU a sequential machine. Next: specialize bistable storage for density — where SRAM and DRAM diverge.

title: The Memory Hierarchy Begins
content:
A D flip-flop (Post 9) is a fine memory element — and expensive per bit: on the order of twenty transistors once clocking, reset, and scan land. A few registers are fine. Gigabytes of main memory that way are not. Two cell designs split the tradeoff: SRAM for speed close to the CPU, DRAM for density farther out.
SRAM: Fast, Stable, Area-Heavy# Static RAM uses the same bistable feedback idea as a latch, packed as a 6-transistor (6T) cell: two cross-coupled inverters hold the bit; two access transistors read and write. With power on, it holds indefinitely — no refresh. Six transistors per bit burn area, so SRAM shows up as cache (Phase 3): small enough that the cost is acceptable, fast enough that no refresh and non-destructive reads matter.
DRAM: Dense, Cheap, High-Maintenance# Dynamic RAM stores the bit as charge on a capacitor, gated by one transistor (1T1C). One transistor instead of six is the density win — and why main memory is DRAM. The cost is in the name: capacitors leak. Commodity parts require every cell refreshed inside a ~64 ms window at normal temperature, or the value fades into ambiguity. Refresh burns bandwidth and complicates the memory controller; it is the price of density. Reads are also destructive — sensing the tiny charge disturbs it — so every read is followed by a rewrite. SRAM has neither problem.
Door out: Robert H. Dennard’s one-transistor DRAM cell (U.S. Patent 3,387,286, 1968) — the 1T1C idea that made dense main memory practical.
The Hierarchy This Sets Up# Registers (flops) at the top: fastest, smallest, most expensive per bit. SRAM cache next. DRAM main memory below. Disk/SSD below that. The pyramid is not decoration — it is transistor-count-vs-speed repeated at every level. Phase 3’s caches build on this; Phase 5’s Memory Wall is what happens when the CPU–DRAM gap, set by exactly this tradeoff, widens faster than caching can hide.

title: Instruction Sets
content:
An Instruction Set Architecture (ISA) is the contract between software and hardware: which operations exist, how they are encoded in bits, and what those bits mean. It is a specification, not a chip. x86, ARM, and RISC-V are ISAs — many different chips can implement the same one and still run the same binaries.
That split — architecture (what software sees) versus microarchitecture (how the silicon is built) — is the spine of this phase. Pipelines, caches, and out-of-order cores all live under the ISA. Software does not have to know.
Two Philosophies: CISC and RISC# CISC (Complex Instruction Set Computing) — the lineage behind x86 — packs a lot into each instruction: variable length, rich addressing modes, arithmetic that can touch memory directly. Fewer instructions per program; a harder decoder.
RISC (Reduced Instruction Set Computing) goes the other way: fixed-length instructions, a strict load/store model (ALU ops on registers only), uniform fields. More instructions per program; each one simple enough to fetch and decode predictably, stage after stage. That uniformity is why pipelining (Post 13) became tractable on RISC first — a fixed-width instruction is far easier to stage than a CISC instruction whose length is unknown until you have already started decoding it.
Concretely: a typical RISC instruction is 32 bits with fields in fixed places. An x86 instruction can run from 1 byte to 15, with optional prefixes — dense and powerful, expensive to decode at high throughput.
Try this now. The mini-CPU below is a tiny ISA: 4-bit opcode, 4-bit operand, sixteen words of memory. Step the guided 8-instruction program and watch fetch / decode / execute move A and memory — the same contract this post just named, small enough to hold in one screen.
Open lab in new tab ↗ Why x86 Persisted Anyway# If RISC is simpler to pipeline, why does x86 still dominate desktop and server? Compatibility and decades of engineering investment — not raw elegance. Modern x86 chips translate CISC instructions into simpler, RISC-like internal micro-ops, then run those on a RISC-style core behind a CISC front end (Post 19). The debate is less a clean binary than the labels suggest.
Next: build an actual datapath — the physical structure an ISA executes on.
Door out: David A. Patterson and David R. Ditzel, “The Case for the Reduced Instruction Set Computer” (Computer Architecture News, 1980) — the classic argument that launched the RISC side of this split.

title: Datapath Design
content:
An ISA (Post 11) is a contract. A datapath is the hardware that carries it out. The simplest version — a single-cycle datapath — finishes one whole instruction per clock tick: fetch, decode, execute, write-back, done. Real CPUs are not built this way today. It is still the clearest way to see how Phase 2’s pieces connect.
One Instruction, One Clock# The pieces: a program counter (Post 9’s flip-flops) holding the next instruction address; instruction memory indexed by that PC; a register file for operands and results; an ALU (Post 8) for the operation; data memory for loads and stores; and a control unit that reads the opcode and drives every mux and enable.
Take ADD. The PC indexes instruction memory. The control unit sees a register-register ADD. Two source registers feed the ALU; the ALU result writes the destination; the PC advances. Fetch, decode, register read, ALU, write-back, PC update — all inside one clock period.
Try this now. Step the mini-CPU below through its guided program. Each Step is one of those pieces in slow motion — fetch into IR, decode the opcode, execute into A and memory — the same path this post just named, small enough to watch.
Open lab in new tab ↗ The Constraint That Forces Pipelining# That clock period must be long enough for the slowest instruction’s full path — even instructions that never touch data memory. Every ADD therefore runs at the speed of the worst case. Throughput sits on the floor.
Pipelining answers that constraint: cut the long path into stages, clock each stage for its worst case, and let different instructions occupy different stages at once. Same ISA. Far more work finished per second. That is the next post — and the central idea of classical microarchitecture.

title: Pipelining
content:
The single-cycle datapath (Post 12) leaves throughput on the table: every instruction waits for the slowest possible path. Pipelining splits execution into stages and lets multiple instructions occupy different stages at once.
Five Stages, Overlapped# A classic RISC pipeline: IF (fetch), ID (decode / register read), EX (ALU), MEM (load/store), WB (write back). Pipeline registers (Post 9 again) latch results between stages each clock.
While instruction N is in EX, N+1 can be in ID and N+2 in IF. In steady state a new instruction completes every cycle — even though each one still takes five cycles start to finish. Latency stays; throughput rises. That distinction shows up everywhere after this.
Try this now. Step the mini-CPU below once per instruction — that is the single-cycle habit Post 12 made visible. Pipelining’s claim is throughput: the same fetch / decode / execute pieces overlapping across instructions, not one whole instruction per tick. Feel the sequential Step, then read the hazard section knowing why real pipelines cannot stay that simple.
Open lab in new tab ↗ Hazards: Where Independence Breaks# Instructions are rarely independent.
Data hazards — an instruction needs a value a previous, still-in-flight instruction has not finished writing. Forwarding (bypassing) routes the ALU result straight from a later pipeline register back into EX, skipping the register file, so the dependent instruction often needs no stall. Forwarding cannot close every gap: a load followed immediately by a use still needs a stall (a bubble) until the MEM stage finishes.
Control hazards — branches. The pipeline does not know taken/not-taken, or the target, until late — but following instructions have already been fetched. On a taken branch those must be flushed. Cycles spent on the wrong path are wasted.
What Those Costs Force Next# Misprediction flushes are expensive — which is why branch prediction (Post 14) exists: guess early and accurately enough that flushes become rare. The load-use stall is why out-of-order execution (Post 16) exists: stall only the waiting instruction, not the whole pipeline, and let independent work behind it run.

title: Branch Prediction
content:
A mispredicted branch flushes everything fetched down the wrong path. On a deep pipeline that can cost well over ten cycles. Post 13 left that cost on the table; this post is the answer: guess direction (and target) early enough that flushes become rare.
Static Guessing Is Not Enough# Static rules — always not-taken, or “backward branches (loops) are taken” — cost no hardware and miss a lot of real code. Branch behavior depends on history a fixed rule cannot see.
Dynamic predictors track outcomes at runtime. A loop that runs 100 times takes its backward branch 99 times; a predictor that remembers “taken last time” gets almost every iteration right.
The 2-Bit Saturating Counter# The classic building block: four states — strongly/weakly not-taken, weakly/strongly taken. Each resolved outcome nudges the counter one step toward what actually happened (saturating at the ends). Prediction is the top bit.
Why not one bit? A 1-bit “last outcome” flips after a single anomaly — then mispredicts the next normal iteration too. Two bits need two consecutive anomalies before flipping, so a loop’s final not-taken exit does not poison the next run of the loop.
Where to Fetch Next# Direction is only half. For a taken branch, fetch also needs a target before the branch is fully decoded. A Branch Target Buffer (BTB) is a small cache, indexed by instruction address, remembering the last resolved target. On a hit, fetch can jump speculatively next cycle.
Real predictors combine counter tables (often with global history) and a BTB; high-end chips go further. The 2-bit counter is still the conceptual core — and small enough to trace by hand. The mini-CPU lab below has no predictor, pipeline or cache, but you can step a loop’s JZ and, on paper, move a 2-bit counter for that branch each iteration.

title: Caches
content:
Post 10 set up the memory hierarchy: registers, SRAM cache, DRAM, disk — capacity traded for speed at every step. Caches are where that tradeoff carries every CPU’s performance. The premise is one empirical fact about real programs: locality.
Why Caches Work at All# Temporal locality — a location just touched is likely to be touched again soon (loop variables, hot code). Spatial locality — nearby locations are likely next (arrays, sequential fetch). Caches keep recently used data close, and fetch whole lines (often 64 bytes) on a miss, betting neighbors arrive soon.
Lookup splits an address into offset (byte in the line), index (which set), and tag (is the line present actually the one we want?).
Where a Line Can Live# Direct-mapped — one possible slot per address. Fast check; conflict misses when two hot addresses share an index and thrash each other.
Fully associative — any line, any slot. No conflict misses; every access compares every tag. Does not scale.
Set-associative — the practical middle: index picks a small set (say 8 ways); tags checked only there. Most of the flexibility, far less hardware than a full scan. Almost every real cache sits here.
Multicore: Coherence as the New Constraint# One core, one private cache: fine. Many cores, each with a cache: core A writes a line core B still holds — without a protocol, B reads stale forever. MESI (Modified, Exclusive, Shared, Invalid) is the classic answer: tag every line with a state, and communicate transitions (bus snoop or directory) so a write invalidates or updates copies elsewhere.
Coherence is not free, and its cost grows with core count — one reason “just add cores” (Post 17) has diminishing returns of its own, separate from ILP limits.
Door out: M. V. Wilkes, “Slave Memories and Dynamic Storage Allocation” (IEEE Transactions on Electronic Computers, 1965) — early statement of the cache idea as a fast slave store beside slower main memory.

title: Out-of-Order Execution
content:
Post 13’s load-use hazard stalls an in-order pipeline behind one waiting instruction — even when later instructions are independent and ready. Out-of-order execution answers that constraint: run independent work whenever operands are ready; enforce program order only where architecture requires it.
False Dependencies and Register Renaming# Not every “dependency” is real. If instruction A writes R1 and later instruction B also writes R1 for an unrelated result, no value flows between them — the ISA simply has few architectural register names, and the compiler reused one. That is a name (false) dependency, not a true data dependency.
Register renaming gives the CPU many more physical registers than the ISA exposes, and maps each write to a fresh physical register at decode. A’s “R1” becomes P17; B’s later “R1” becomes P42. No false conflict; both can proceed.
Issue When Ready, Commit In Order# Renamed instructions wait in reservation stations until real operands arrive (by value or by tag from a producer still in flight). The moment operands are ready, the instruction can issue to an execution unit — regardless of original program order. That is the out-of-order part.
Architectural effects still must look in-order: visible registers, memory, exceptions. The reorder buffer (ROB) tracks every in-flight instruction in program order and only retires results to architectural state in that order, even when execution finished at different times.
Tomasulo’s Core Idea# “Execute whenever ready, commit strictly in order” — the pattern often credited to Robert Tomasulo’s algorithm for the IBM System/360 Model 91 floating-point unit (published 1967) — is the conceptual core of essentially every high-performance out-of-order CPU since. It is also expensive: renaming tables, reservation stations, and the ROB cost area and power. Adding more of that machinery has diminishing returns — the wall the next post hits head-on.
Open lab in new tab ↗ Door out: R. M. Tomasulo, “An Efficient Algorithm for Exploiting Multiple Arithmetic Units” (IBM Journal of Research and Development, 1967) — the primary paper behind modern out-of-order issue and rename.

title: Superscalar & Multicore
content:
Out-of-order issue, deeper pipelines, wider superscalar width — everything so far in this phase extracts more Instruction-Level Parallelism (ILP) from one instruction stream. By the mid-2000s that approach hit a ceiling hard enough to change strategy.
Two Walls at Once# Real programs do not offer unlimited independent work. Branches, true data dependencies, and memory latency cap how many instructions can run in parallel from a single stream. Bigger ROBs, more reservation stations, wider issue: shrinking returns for growing area and power. That is an architectural wall.
At the same time, dynamic power scales roughly with capacitance, frequency, and voltage squared (P ≈ CV²f). Pushing clocks higher to compensate for ILP’s dwindling gains ran into heat — the clock-speed wall Post 36 covers in detail. Two independent ceilings, mid-2000s, neither with a clean solo fix.
Wide Instead of Fast# The pivot: stop making one core do more per cycle; put multiple, somewhat simpler cores on the same die, each with its own stream. Chip throughput can keep climbing while per-core complexity and clocks level off — if there is parallel work to hand those cores.
“Faster” changed meaning. A single-threaded program does not automatically win on eight cores versus four; it still runs on one core at roughly the same clock. Multicore gain appears only for workloads written (or compiled) for multiple threads. The ILP era mostly gave single-thread speedups “for free” each generation; this era demands parallel-aware software.
Where the Pivot Points# The same force — many simpler units instead of one complex one — is the philosophy behind GPUs (Phase 9) taken further. It is also why coordinating parallel work correctly becomes a first-class problem in real-time systems (Phase 4) and distributed systems (Phase 7): waiting for the next chip to make one thread faster is no longer the main growth path.
Door out: Kunle Olukotun, Basem A. Nayfeh, Lance Hammond, Ken Wilson, and Kunyung Chang, “The Case for a Single-Chip Multiprocessor” (ASPLOS 1996) — an early, explicit argument for putting multiple cores on one die as ILP returns flatten.

title: Mainframes to Minicomputers to Microprocessors
content:
ENIAC (Phase 1) occupied about 1,800 square feet and weighed roughly 30 tons. A phone CPU outperforms it by orders of magnitude on a fingertip. That collapse was not one leap — three eras, each answering differently: who gets a computer, and how many exist?
Mainframes: One Machine, Shared# 1950s–60s: room-filling machines for universities, corporations, governments — shared through batch processing (Post 21). IBM’s System/360 (1964) mattered beyond scale: a family of compatible machines across a performance range, same software. Deliberate separation of ISA (Post 11) from the box underneath, so a customer’s code survived a hardware upgrade. Gene Amdahl, Gerrit Blaauw, and Fred Brooks drove that architecture.
Minicomputers: A Department Can Afford One# 1970s: DEC’s PDP-11 (1970) and kin shrank the machine to something a department — not a whole institution — could buy and run without a central bureau. By May 1990, DEC counted more than 600,000 PDP-11s installed. The ISA’s orthogonal addressing and clean encoding shaped later design, including habits in C (Post 27), which grew up with Unix (Post 22) largely on PDP-11 hardware.
Microprocessors: The CPU on One Die# The discontinuity: fabricate the whole CPU on one integrated circuit instead of wiring racks of discrete parts. Intel’s 4004 (1971), built for a calculator, is usually credited as the first commercial single-chip CPU — 4-bit, about 2,300 transistors, up to roughly 740 kHz. Weak by any modern measure; the direct ancestor of the 8080, the Z80, and the x86 line in the next post.
Why the Collapse Compounded# Each step tracks fabrication density from Phase 8: more transistors, less area, lower cost. Mainframes were thousands of components on backplanes; microprocessors compressed that structure onto silicon. Computing moved from institutional resource to departmental tool to personal (then embedded) device — the same scaling curve Phase 8 follows into what a modern process node actually means.
Open lab in new tab ↗ Door out: G. M. Amdahl, G. A. Blaauw, and F. P. Brooks Jr., “Architecture of the IBM System/360” (IBM Journal of Research and Development, 1964) — the primary statement of a compatible machine family and the ISA/implementation split.

title: The x86 vs RISC Split
content:
Post 11 named CISC and RISC as philosophies. This post is what happened when they competed commercially — and why the “cleaner” ISA did not simply win.
The RISC Argument# Early 1980s: RISC as a reaction to CISC complexity — Berkeley work toward SPARC, Stanford toward MIPS, IBM work that fed POWER/PowerPC. The claim was empirical: complex CISC ops were often barely used in compiled code, while the decode hardware they needed burned silicon and complicated the pipelines this phase already covered. Strip the ISA to simple, fixed-length, uniform instructions; spend the silicon on registers, faster pipelines, better caches instead.
MIPS, SPARC, and PowerPC all shipped. For a stretch they beat x86 on pure compute benchmarks, especially workstations and servers.
Why x86 Kept the Floor# x86’s edge was never elegance — it was the software already sitting on IBM PC compatibility. Once that became the desktop standard, an enormous installed base only ran on x86. Backward compatibility became a moat: new chips had to run old binaries, so the ISA could not be cleanly redesigned RISC-style — only extended, wart by wart, while Intel and later AMD made the implementation fast despite the surface.
The real resolution: modern x86 does not execute CISC ops directly in the out-of-order core. A decoder translates each x86 instruction into one or more fixed-format internal micro-operations (µops) — RISC-like — and those flow through the reservation stations, ROB, and execution units from Post 16. Outside: CISC-compatible. Inside: a RISC-style pipeline under a translation layer.
The Pattern to Keep# Winning ISAs are rarely won on technical merit alone. Compatibility, ecosystem lock-in, and manufacturing scale routinely beat cleaner paper architecture. The same dynamic shows up next with ARM’s licensing model versus RISC-V’s open ISA — the business model around an instruction set can matter as much as the encoding.
Open lab in new tab ↗ Door out: David A. Patterson and David R. Ditzel, “The Case for the Reduced Instruction Set Computer” (Computer Architecture News, 1980) — the manifesto of the RISC side of this commercial fight.

title: ARM and RISC-V: The Architecture Landscape Today
content:
The x86-versus-RISC fight (Post 19) mostly settled desktop and server by the late 1990s. Competition did not end — it moved. Mobile, embedded, and edge care more about watts than single-thread peak, and the business model around an ISA turned out to matter as much as the encoding.
ARM: License the ISA, Don’t Build the Fab# ARM Holdings designs the ISA and licenses it — ready-to-fabricate cores, or architecture licenses that let a company design its own ARM-compatible core (Apple’s silicon is the standout of the latter). The model spread the ISA across many manufacturers without ARM running a fab.
Technically, ARM entered the mobile era already tuned for power efficiency — RISC-lineage simple decode meeting a market that, for the first time at mass scale, cared about performance-per-watt. That was not luck; it was decades of that design discipline meeting battery-powered devices.
RISC-V: Open Instead of Licensed# RISC-V (work starting around 2010 at UC Berkeley, with Krste Asanović, David Patterson, and colleagues among the named drivers) goes further: the ISA is open and royalty-free. Implement a core without negotiating with a controlling vendor. That matters most where deep customization or zero ISA licensing cost is the point — embedded systems, and accelerators that want custom instructions on a RISC-V base without asking permission.
Same Lesson, One Layer Deeper# Rough map: x86 still owns much of desktop and server on compatibility inertia. ARM owns mobile, with real server and laptop inroads (custom cloud ARM; Apple Silicon). RISC-V is earlier commercially, growing fastest where royalty-free flexibility beats a mature software stack.
Post 19’s pattern again: the winner in a segment is not always the “best” ISA in isolation — it is the one whose economics fit what that segment buys. ARM won mobile on watts and a licensing model phone makers could customize under. RISC-V bets that “free and open” beats even that for a growing set of cases. Whether that reaches x86 or ARM scale is still open.
Open lab in new tab ↗ Door out: The RISC-V Instruction Set Manual (riscv.org) — the living primary specification for the open ISA this post names; start with the unprivileged ISA volume.

title: Batch Processing and the Birth of the Operating System
content:
The mainframes of Post 18 did not run an operating system in any sense we would recognize. Someone loaded a program, ran it, waited, then loaded the next. That works for one user with exclusive access. It falls apart the moment multiple jobs must share an expensive machine — which, given mainframe cost, happened almost immediately.
Idle Time Was the Constraint# Early operation meant a human loading a punch-card deck, running it, collecting output, loading the next — while the CPU sat idle through every setup and teardown. Batch processing automated the sequencing: submit a stack of jobs, and a resident program (an early “monitor”) loaded and ran each one in turn, with no human between jobs.
That resident monitor is the direct ancestor of the operating system. Narrow job — load, start, detect finish, load next — but it is the first piece of system software distinct from any user’s program, running continuously to manage the machine on behalf of whichever job is executing.
Scheduling Becomes Policy# As batch systems matured, job control languages let a submitted job name resources, failure handling, and output routing; queues let jobs be prioritized instead of run in strict submission order. Priority, resource allocation, and scheduling policy show up here as real OS concerns — not informal operator judgment.
What Batch Could Not Give# No interactivity. A job ran start to finish with no chance to intervene, inspect intermediate state, or redirect. A bug often surfaced only after the full run — sometimes hours later, after burning an expensive allocation. For exploratory work, that turnaround was a hard productivity ceiling.
Try this now. Boot the VM below, click the screen, then run whoami, uname, and ls. That prompt is the opposite of a batch deck — you intervene now, inspect state, and redirect. Time-sharing (next post) is what made this illusion shareable.
Open lab in new tab ↗ Solving it required something batch architecture could not provide: multiple users active at the same time, each with the illusion of a dedicated session. That is time-sharing — not just automating job sequencing, but interleaving simultaneously active programs until the switching is invisible. The next post picks up there.

title: Time-Sharing and the Unix Lineage
content:
Batch processing (Post 21) solved throughput — keep the expensive CPU busy between jobs. It did nothing for interactivity. Time-sharing, emerging in the early-to-mid 1960s, solved a different constraint: let multiple users interact simultaneously, each with the illusion of having the machine alone.
The Core Trick: Rapid Switching# A CPU is fast relative to human reaction time. Switch between many users’ processes many times per second — each gets a small slice — and no one perceives the gaps. Software-scheduling analog of Post 9’s clocked logic: discrete, rapid switching that looks continuous, even though only one process runs on a single core at any instant.
Multics (MULTiplexed Information and Computing Service), a joint MIT / Bell Labs / GE project planned from 1964 and publicly described in 1965, was hugely ambitious — hierarchical file systems, dynamic linking, fine-grained access control that took decades to become standard elsewhere. It was also, by most accounts, over-engineered for the hardware of its time, and commercially it struggled.
From Multics to Unix# Bell Labs pulled out of Multics in 1969. Ken Thompson and Dennis Ritchie, who had worked on it, kept iterating at a much smaller scale — deliberately simpler, on far less powerful hardware (initially a spare PDP-7). The result was Unix: a time-sharing OS built around a small set of composable ideas — “everything is a file,” small single-purpose programs connected by pipes, and a portable design once rewritten in C (Post 27 covers that language, largely by the same people).
Portability mattered. Unix was not locked to one manufacturer’s box the way many contemporaries were, so it could spread across vendors with modest porting effort — a structural advantage over systems tied to a single product line.
Try this now. Boot the VM below, click the black screen for keyboard focus, then run uname, whoami, and ls — a living Unix-lineage shell, not a diagram of one.
Open lab in new tab ↗ The Split: BSD and System V# Unix’s licensing history is tangled (AT&T’s antitrust-related restrictions meant it could not freely commercialize Unix for a long stretch, which paradoxically encouraged wide academic distribution). It eventually split into two major lineages: BSD (Berkeley Software Distribution), with substantial new work including much of the TCP/IP stack in Phase 6, and AT&T’s commercial System V line. Both cross-pollinated for years. Modern systems still trace design decisions to one branch or the other — macOS’s kernel has deep BSD lineage; much enterprise Unix descended more directly from System V.
Where This Leads# Unix’s ideas — and, eventually, Unix-derived or Unix-inspired code — are the direct ancestor of both Linux and macOS, which between them run the overwhelming majority of servers, workstations, and increasingly mobile and embedded devices today. Getting from “AT&T’s proprietary Unix” to “the free, openly developed Linux running most of the internet” required a separate ideological and legal movement — the GNU project — which the next post covers. Distinct story from Unix’s technical lineage, even though the two ultimately combined into one dominant stack.
Door out: Dennis M. Ritchie and Ken Thompson, “The UNIX Time-Sharing System” (Communications of the ACM, 1974) — the classic primary statement of Unix’s design.

title: The GNU Movement and Linux
content:
By the early 1980s, Unix (Post 22) was technically excellent and increasingly proprietary — AT&T asserting commercial control, academic and hobbyist access tightening. Richard Stallman’s response, starting in 1983, was not primarily a technical fix. It was ideological and legal: build a completely free (as in freedom, not just price) Unix replacement from scratch, and back it with a license designed to keep it that way.
GNU: Userland Without a Kernel# GNU — “GNU’s Not Unix” — set out to build a complete, Unix-compatible operating system where every component was free software: usable, modifiable, and redistributable, including redistribution of your own modifications. Over the following decade the project produced essential infrastructure: GCC (still one of the most widely used compilers — Post 28), Bash, GNU coreutils, Emacs, and much more.
What GNU did not have, for years, was a working kernel. Its planned kernel, GNU Hurd, ran into serious technical difficulties and never reached broad practical usability. Complete userland; no kernel underneath it for real hardware.
The GPL: Copyright Turned Outward# Stallman’s other major contribution was the GNU General Public License (GPL) — a “copyleft” license with a deliberate property: if you distribute software incorporating GPL-licensed code, you must make your modified source available under the same terms. Copyright, normally a tool for restricting redistribution, used to guarantee that freedom propagates through every derivative — rather than being quietly closed by a downstream commercial fork.
Linux Fills the Gap# In 1991, Finnish student Linus Torvalds started a kernel as a personal project for his own PC. He released it that year under a restrictive non-commercial license of his own, then — critically — relicensed it under the GPL in early 1992. That combination was the missing piece: GNU had mature userland with no practical kernel; Linux was a functional kernel with essentially no userland. Together, GNU utilities on the Linux kernel formed a complete, freely licensed, Unix-compatible system — commonly called “Linux,” though “GNU/Linux” is the more historically precise name for the combination (to Stallman’s occasional public frustration).
Try this now. Boot the VM below, click the screen, then try uname, whoami, and ls — you are on the GNU/Linux side of that combination, in your browser.
Open lab in new tab ↗ Why This Combination Won# The GPL’s structure meant companies could build commercial products around Linux without quietly closing the underlying platform — kernel modifications had to remain available as source under the same terms. That built sustained trust and, eventually, sustained corporate contribution: firms could rely on the platform staying open rather than being captured by a single competitor. Free, open to commercial use, legally structured to stay that way — a large part of why Linux became the dominant kernel under servers, cloud infrastructure, Android, and much of the modern internet’s backbone, well beyond one student’s personal project.
Door out: The GNU General Public License (Free Software Foundation) — the primary legal text that made copyleft enforceable; read alongside Stallman’s GNU Manifesto (1985) for the project’s stated goal.

title: Virtual Memory and Multitasking
content:
Time-sharing (Post 22) requires multiple processes to run — apparently simultaneously — on one machine. Immediate problem: if every process could freely read and write any physical address, one buggy or malicious program could corrupt another’s data, or the OS itself. Virtual memory prevents that by giving every process the illusion of owning the entire address space, while the OS manages the truth underneath.
The Core Illusion# Every process sees a full virtual address space — on a 64-bit system, far larger than physical RAM. When it references a virtual address, hardware (a Memory Management Unit, or MMU) translates to a physical address via a page table the OS maintains. Two processes can both reference “virtual address 0x1000” and hit two different physical frames — neither can see the other’s memory, even though from inside each process it looks like ordinary, exclusive ownership.
Pages, Faults, Swap# Memory is divided into fixed-size pages (commonly 4 KB on many architectures; larger “huge pages” also exist). The page table maps virtual pages to physical frames. Critically, not every virtual page needs a frame at all times — mark it “not present,” and a reference traps into the OS as a page fault. The OS can load the page from disk (lazy bring-in of code and data), or treat it as a genuine error (accessing memory never granted — one common path to a segmentation fault).
The same mechanism enables swapping: under memory pressure, write a cold page to disk, mark it not-present, free the frame. The system behaves as if it has more RAM than it physically does — at disk-speed cost if that page is touched again. Abundant RAM makes heavy swapping less common than it once was; the mechanism remains fundamental.
Isolation as Security# Beyond enabling multitasking, translation is a security boundary. A process has no mechanism to address another process’s physical memory — no valid virtual address in its page table maps there. Memory corruption in one well-behaved, sandboxed process does not (in principle) let it read or corrupt an unrelated process; isolation is hardware-checked address translation, not convention.
Where This Leads# Virtual memory gives every process its own isolated address space — a strong guarantee, and a heavyweight one: own kernel structures, own page tables, full context-switch cost between them. Containers (the next post) ask: can you get most of the practical isolation processes need, without paying for an entirely separate kernel per tenant?

title: Containers and Modern OS Isolation
content:
Virtual memory (Post 24) isolates processes from each other’s memory. It does not isolate them from sharing the same filesystem, process-ID space, or network configuration — a traditional Unix process can still see and sometimes interfere with others in plenty of ways beyond raw RAM. Containers extend isolation across more of that surface, without going all the way to full hardware virtualization.
Full Virtualization: Strong, Heavy# A traditional VM runs a complete guest OS — own kernel, own drivers — on a hypervisor that presents virtualized (or, with hardware assistance, near-native) CPU, memory, storage, and networking. Extremely strong isolation: a guest cannot see the host’s processes or other guests, short of a serious hypervisor bug. Cost is real — each VM boots its own kernel, carries that kernel’s memory footprint, and generally pays slower access to some hardware than running on the host.
Share the Kernel, Isolate the View# Containers take the other trade: every container on a host shares the same kernel — no guest OS boot per instance — while the kernel provides isolation so each container’s view looks separate. Two Linux features do most of the work. Namespaces isolate a process’s view of specific resources — a PID namespace makes a container see only its own process tree (process 1 inside is not PID 1 on the host); a network namespace gives private interfaces and routing; a mount namespace gives a private filesystem view. Cgroups (control groups) limit and account for CPU, memory, and I/O so one container cannot starve others on the same host.
The lineage is older than the buzzword: chroot (changing a process’s apparent filesystem root, early 1980s) was limited filesystem isolation decades earlier; cgroups and modern namespaces generalize that idea across more of a process’s world.
Why the Tradeoff Won at Scale# Because containers share the host kernel, they typically start in a fraction of a second (no kernel boot) and carry a much smaller footprint per instance — no duplicated kernel image or kernel-level caches. That efficiency is why they became the default packaging and deployment unit for modern cloud infrastructure: far more containers than VMs on the same hardware, which matters at the scale distributed systems (Phase 7) actually run.
Tradeoff: shared kernel means a serious enough kernel vulnerability can, in principle, break container isolation in a way that is structurally harder under separate-kernel virtualization. Most production systems accept that deliberately, sometimes layering more sandboxing on top. Post 45’s Kubernetes discussion picks up here: once you have a lightweight, fast-starting isolation unit, the next problem is orchestrating thousands of them across a fleet.

title: From Machine Code to Assembly
content:
Every instruction in Phase 3 — datapath, pipeline, ISA — ultimately exists as raw binary: bit patterns hardware decodes directly. Nobody writes programs that way at scale. Assembly is the first abstraction on top of that binary. Understanding what it buys — and what it does not change — matters for everything downstream in software history.
What Assembly Actually Is# Assembly gives every instruction a human-readable mnemonic — ADD, LDA, JMP — corresponding one-to-one with a machine-code bit pattern. It is not “higher-level” the way Post 27’s languages are; there is no abstraction over the underlying hardware ops. Every assembly instruction maps to exactly one machine instruction. What you get is readability and symbolic reference: write LDI instead of remembering opcode 0101; in a full assembler, write a label and let it compute the jump target instead of recalculating byte addresses by hand. (The mini-CPU lab’s tiny assembler has no labels; there you write the addresses yourself.)
The Assembler’s Job# An assembler translates assembly text into machine code — resolving labels into addresses, mnemonics into opcode bits, packing operands into the ISA’s encoding fields (Post 11). Mechanical, largely one-to-one. Nothing is being optimized or restructured in any deep sense — unlike what a full compiler (Post 28) does with a high-level language.
Why It Had to Happen# Before assembly, programming meant entering binary or, at best, raw hex or octal opcodes — unmanageable beyond trivial programs, nearly impossible to debug or modify at scale. Symbolic labels alone were transformative: insert or remove an instruction, and you no longer recalculate every jump by hand — the assembler does the arithmetic.
Where Assembly Still Matters# Modern software is overwhelmingly written in higher-level languages and compiled through the pipeline in Post 28. Assembly has not disappeared. Engineers still drop to it to reason about exactly what a compiler produced (hot loops, security review, reverse engineering), or to write the lowest layers — boot code, interrupt handlers, parts of a kernel — where instruction-level control is required and higher abstractions would obscure or prevent it.
Try this now. The mini-CPU lab below is the most direct hands-on connection in the series: Assemble the guided program, then Step — each mnemonic (LDI, ADD, STA, OUT) maps one-to-one onto opcode bits, exactly as this post describes. Nothing more abstract than that.
