title: High-Level Languages: FORTRAN, COBOL, Lisp, C
content:
Assembly (Post 26) is a one-to-one layer over machine code — better than raw binary, still forcing the programmer to think in instructions, registers, and manual layout. High-level languages introduced something different: abstractions that do not map one-to-one onto hardware at all. Express what to compute; a compiler (Post 28) figures out how.
FORTRAN: Formula Translation# FORTRAN (1957, IBM) was built for scientific and engineering computation — the name means “Formula Translation.” Write X = A * B + C instead of a sequence of arithmetic instructions with explicit register allocation. That required real compiler cleverness. Early skepticism held that compiled code could not compete with hand-written assembly; FORTRAN’s compiler had to prove that wrong through aggressive optimization, and largely did.
COBOL: Business, Not Science# COBOL (1959–60, CODASYL) targeted a different domain: payroll, accounting, inventory — business data processing, not science. Grace Hopper did not write COBOL herself, but her earlier FLOW-MATIC was a primary influence, and she is often credited as the “mother of COBOL” for that influence and her advocacy. Design choice: verbose, English-like syntax (ADD SALARY TO TOTAL-PAY), meant to be readable by non-programmer analysts and auditors. Legacy is enormous and still underappreciated: a significant fraction of core banking, insurance, and government systems still run COBOL written decades ago — rewriting mission-critical financial systems is expensive and risky enough that many organizations keep maintaining the original instead.
Lisp: A Different Paradigm# Lisp (1958, John McCarthy) left FORTRAN and COBOL’s imperative style entirely — functions as first-class values, and a minimal uniform syntax where code and data share the same list structure. Not just style: programs that construct and execute other programs at runtime became foundational to decades of AI and symbolic computation, and still influence functional features in mainstream languages today.
C: Systems Programming, Close to the Machine# C (1972, Dennis Ritchie, developed alongside Unix — Post 22) took yet another trade: high-level enough for real productivity over assembly, close enough to hardware that an entire OS kernel could be written in it — unusual then. Pointer arithmetic, minimal runtime, predictable mapping to machine ops made Unix portable: port the C compiler to a new machine, not rewrite the OS in each target’s assembly.
The Common Thread# Each language optimized for a different priority — FORTRAN for numerical expression, COBOL for business readability, Lisp for symbolic abstraction, C for systems-level control — and each still shapes design today. What they share, and what makes any of them usable, is a compiler that turns the abstraction into efficient machine code without the programmer doing that translation by hand. That process — and what “optimization” concretely means — is the next post.
Door out: Dennis M. Ritchie, “The Development of the C Language” (HOPL-II / ACM) — primary account of C’s design beside Unix; for Lisp’s founding statement, see John McCarthy’s early CACM papers on recursive functions of symbolic expressions.

title: Compilers, JIT, and Modern Language Runtimes
content:
Post 27 covered why high-level languages exist. This post is the machinery that makes them usable: the compiler, translating source into something a real CPU (Phase 3) can execute.
The Classical Pipeline (Short)# Lexer → tokens. Parser → Abstract Syntax Tree. Semantic analysis catches what grammar alone cannot (types, undeclared names). Most real compilers then lower to an Intermediate Representation (IR) — more uniform than source syntax, still independent of any target ISA — where the optimizer works: dead-code elimination, loop-invariant hoisting, inlining, and dozens of other transformations that preserve behavior while cutting wasted work. Code generation emits target instructions and does register allocation (which values live in scarce physical registers versus spilling to memory).
That is the spine. The encyclopedia of every pass is not the point — the constraint is: source abstractions do not run; something must lower them, and that something can run before execution or during it.
Ahead-of-Time vs Just-in-Time# Run the whole pipeline once before the program ever executes: Ahead-of-Time (AOT) — C and traditional FORTRAN. Just-in-Time (JIT) — Java, JavaScript, and kin — starts with an interpreter or a fast baseline compiler, then at runtime finds hot paths and recompiles those with heavier optimization.
The JIT’s advantage is information an AOT compiler never had: observed branches, argument types, actual hot loops — optimizations unsafe to assume without that data. Cost is real: compilation burns cycles during execution, and the first seconds often run slower than steady state — classic warm-up.
Runtimes: More Than Compilation# Managed languages (Java, C#, and to varying degrees JavaScript and Python) pair the compiler with a broader runtime — most consequentially automatic memory management via garbage collection, freeing programmers from tracking every allocation’s lifetime (a major bug source in C). Complexity shifts into the runtime: manual effort traded for overhead and, historically, less predictable pauses. That tension is exactly why Posts 29–30 treat “real-time” and “garbage-collected managed runtime” as frequently at odds.
See It Live# The VM terminal below is a real Linux system, but a minimal BusyBox one: it has no C compiler (gcc answers gcc: not found). It can still show both sides of this post. Run hexdump -C /bin/busybox | head -2: the file starts 7f 45 4c 46 — 0x7f then “ELF”, the executable format a compiler and linker produce, built ahead of time on another machine long before you booted the VM. Then give an interpreter the same work: echo 'BEGIN{s=0; for(i=1;i<=1000000;i++) s+=i; print s}' > /tmp/sum.awk, then time awk -f /tmp/sum.awk. It prints 500000500000 after several seconds (about 6 s in our runs; your browser will differ), because awk executes every iteration at run time — a loop an optimizing compiler can reduce to a constant before the program ever runs.

title: Real-Time Systems and Deterministic Scheduling
content:
Everything so far in Phase 4 — batch, time-sharing, virtual memory, containers — optimizes for throughput, fairness, or efficient sharing. None of it hard-guarantees when a given piece of work finishes. Real-time systems care about that guarantee. “Fast” is a different property from “real-time” — a distinction that trips people up constantly.
Fast Is Not Deterministic# A general-purpose scheduler (Posts 21–25) optimizes for good average-case responsiveness and fair sharing — usually quite fast in the common case. “Usually fast” is not “always finishes within a specified deadline, no exceptions.” Cache effects, interrupt handling, or garbage-collection pauses (Post 28) can stretch a delay. For most apps, occasional variance does not matter. For a real-time system, it can be the entire ballgame.
Hard vs Soft# A hard deadline: missing it is total system failure — not degraded performance. Flight-control stabilization, airbag deployment — every time, within the window, or the failure can be catastrophic.
A soft deadline: missing it degrades quality but is not outright failure — a dropped video frame under load is unpleasant, not a certification crisis. Strong practical tendency to hit deadlines; not a hardware-enforced guarantee.
Rate-Monotonic Scheduling# One classical approach to hard real-time: rate-monotonic scheduling — assign each periodic task a fixed priority from how frequently it must run; shorter period → higher priority. Provably optimal among fixed-priority algorithms for a well-defined class of periodic task sets: if any fixed-priority assignment can meet every deadline for that workload, rate-monotonic will too. A mathematical schedulability bound — exactly the kind of formal property hard real-time systems need to certify against.
Why a Different Kind of OS# Meeting these guarantees requires an OS designed around bounded worst-case timing — a Real-Time Operating System (RTOS) — not the throughput/fairness lineage of Posts 21–25. Interrupt latency must be bounded and known. Memory allocation typically cannot rely on unpredictable-latency mechanisms like a general-purpose GC. Even a mutex needs careful design (priority inheritance) so a low-priority task cannot block a high-priority one for an unbounded time — priority inversion, a classic real-time pitfall.
Revisit the mini-CPU lab through this lens: on simple hardware, every instruction’s timing is deterministic and countable — the predictability RTOS design fights to preserve as systems grow more complex. The next post takes these principles into avionics, industrial control, and embedded deployments where the guarantees are load-bearing.

title: Real-Time Systems in Practice
content:
Post 29 covered the theory: hard vs soft deadlines, rate-monotonic scheduling, why “fast” and “real-time” differ. This post is where those guarantees get deployed — and what building for them looks like in practice.
Avionics: Missed Deadline as Catastrophe# Flight control is the canonical hard-real-time example for good reason. A fly-by-wire stability-augmentation loop reads sensors, computes control-surface adjustments, and issues actuator commands on a fixed, tight cycle. Miss the deadline and control response can become unstable, sometimes within a very short window. Avionics software is built to standards like DO-178C that demand rigorous timing analysis — not “usually meets deadlines,” but evidence that it always does under certified operating conditions (objectives scale by assurance level; the spine is worst-case discipline, not average-case hope).
Industrial Automation: Coordinated Continuous Control# A production line — robotic arms, conveyor timing, quality-control sensors — runs the same closed-loop pattern: sense, compute, actuate, repeat, often on a millisecond cycle. Miss a deadline here and the failure is usually less catastrophic than in avionics, but still serious — a late position command relative to a moving part can mean collision, a dropped piece, or damage to expensive equipment.
The Shared Architecture: Closed-Loop Control# Both domains share a pattern worth naming: sense (current state from sensors), compute (correct response — often a PID or similar control-theory algorithm), actuate (motor signal, surface deflection), repeated on a fixed period. The real-time guarantee covers the entire loop end to end — sensor latency, computation, and actuation all count against the same budget. A blazing control algorithm still fails if sensor I/O or actuator communication injects unpredictable delay elsewhere in that loop.
Why General-Purpose Hardware Often Isn’t Enough# Real-time systems frequently run on dedicated microcontrollers rather than general-purpose CPUs under a general-purpose OS. Simpler, more predictable architecture — often no caches, no out-of-order execution, no speculative branch prediction — deliberately trading away exactly the Phase 3 techniques that make timing less predictable. What Phase 3 treats as a performance win is precisely what a hard-real-time system must design around, or avoid.
Two Labs, One Contrast# This is the one post tagged with both interactive labs, deliberately: the mini-CPU is where deterministic, countable instruction timing on simple hardware is tangible — why simplicity aids certifiability. The VM terminal runs a full general-purpose OS stack — useful for seeing the scheduling and timing variance a hard-real-time system is built to eliminate.

title: Buses 101
content:
Every previous phase built something — logic, a CPU, an operating system. This phase is how those pieces talk. A bus is the shared path among CPU, memory, and I/O, and its design decides how fast a system can move data between the parts Phase 3 and Phase 4 treated as simply “connected.”
Three Signals, One Set of Wires# A classic system bus carries three kinds of signal on shared physical wires. The address bus names the target — its width is the address-space ceiling (32 bits → 4 GB, the wall 32-bit systems hit as memory grew). The data bus carries the value — its width is bandwidth per transaction. The control bus coordinates: direction, validity, clock, interrupts.
Why Sharing Needs a Master# A bus is shared by definition. CPU, DMA controller, I/O device may all want to start a transfer; only one can drive the wires or the voltages fight. Arbitration picks a bus master for the next transaction — request and grant, sometimes with priority so a latency-sensitive DMA is not starved by everyone else. Same fairness problem as Phase 4’s schedulers, one layer down, in hardware.
The Constraint: One Transaction at a Time# Total bandwidth is a hard ceiling the whole machine shares. More devices means more waiting, and less effective bandwidth anyone sees under contention. That is not an implementation detail. It is the constraint the rest of this phase works around — first by making the shared parallel bus faster, then by abandoning the shared wires entirely. Post 32 is that escape: from one parallel bus toward point-to-point serial links that do not force every device to compete for the same copper.

title: From ISA Bus to PCI to PCIe
content:
Post 31’s ceiling: every device contends for the same wires. ISA, then PCI, then PCIe is the engineering around that ceiling — not a catalog of buses, a sequence of constraints. The surprise at the end: going serial (fewer wires) beat staying parallel (more wires).
The Parallel Intuition, and Where It Breaks# ISA (Industry Standard Architecture) was a wide parallel bus: many data lines, one bit each, clocked together. More wires should mean more bandwidth. At modest clocks, it does.
Every wire has slightly different length and capacitance, so bits do not arrive at the same instant — skew. At a slow clock the variance is a small fraction of the period and does not matter. Raise the clock, shrink the period, and the same fixed skew eats the timing margin until the receiver cannot sample every bit on one edge. That is a physical ceiling, not a missed trick. You cannot crank a wide parallel bus indefinitely.
PCI Bought Headroom, Not Escape# PCI (Peripheral Component Interconnect, 1992) was faster than ISA — better arbitration, plug-and-play configuration, more practical bandwidth. It was still a shared parallel bus, still subject to skew as clocks rose. Headroom, not a new architecture.
PCIe Left the Shared Wires# PCI Express (2003) changed the topology. Instead of one shared parallel bus, each device gets a dedicated point-to-point serial link (a lane, or a bundle of lanes) to a switch. One differential pair per direction per lane: nothing to keep in lockstep across a dozen wires, so per-lane clocks can climb far past any parallel bus. Lanes bond (x1, x4, x8, x16) for devices that need more — a GPU takes x16 because it moves far more than a NIC in x1. Unrelated devices no longer share wires, so they no longer wait on each other’s arbitration.
Fewer physical wires. Higher achievable bandwidth. The shared-bus ceiling is gone. Post 33 is how those serial links structure a transfer so the rest of the machine can still mean a read or a write.

title: PCIe Deep Dive
content:
Post 32 covered why PCIe went serial and point-to-point. This post is how a transfer is structured on those links — the layer that matters if you are building hardware that has to speak the fabric, including the Nitefury-based GPU memory work this series comes back to.
Intent, Reliability, Electrons# Three layers, three jobs. The Transaction Layer is where a read, a write, or a completion is born and dies — the layer software thinks in. The Data Link Layer makes delivery reliable: sequence numbers, CRC, retransmission if a packet is corrupted. The Physical Layer is the wire: differential pairs, encoding so the stream stays recoverable, serialization onto copper. Split that way so a custom design can express intent without reinventing electrons.
The Packet Is the Contract# The unit is the Transaction Layer Packet. A TLP names the type (memory read or write, I/O, configuration), the address, the length, and — on a write — the payload. The link layer wraps it with sequence and CRC; the far side checks and retries if needed. From above, it looks like a reliable read or write. The reliability is not magic. It is that wrap.
Lanes Scale Width; Generations Scale Rate# A lane is one differential pair each way — the smallest link. Bond lanes (x1…x16) to multiply bandwidth. Each generation roughly doubles per-lane rate (higher signaling, tighter encoding). Same x16 slot, Gen 5 versus Gen 3: about 4× unidirectional bandwidth (~64 GB/s vs ~16 GB/s) with no extra wires. The serial bet from Post 32 is what made that climb possible.
Why a Custom Fabric Cares# An FPGA memory-fabric card has to live in this stack: form TLPs the root complex and other endpoints will accept, and let established IP handle link reliability and the physical layer. GPUDirect-style peer-to-peer (Post 37) is the same idea taken further — TLPs addressed between two endpoints, CPU out of the data path.
Door out: The PCI Express Base Specification (PCI-SIG) — the living primary for lanes, TLPs, and the layered stack this post names; it is versioned (the Base Spec, not a frozen paper).

title: Memory Buses
content:
PCIe (Posts 32–33) is the path to expansion devices. The memory bus is the path that actually feeds the CPU — DRAM from Post 10 — and its evolution is a running negotiation among bandwidth, latency, and power. The generation names are not the story. The split between those three is.
Both Edges, Not a Faster Clock# DDR — Double Data Rate — transfers on the rising and falling edge. Roughly twice the throughput of a single-data-rate design at the same clock, without doubling frequency (and the signal-integrity problems that come with it). Bandwidth without paying the clock wall first.
Bandwidth Climbed; First-Bit Latency Did Not# Each DDR generation raised peak bandwidth, mostly by faster I/O. Prefetch and, in DDR5, a split into two independent 32-bit subchannels buy more parallelism on the module. What the headline numbers hide: raw access latency — request to first bit — moved far more slowly than bandwidth. DRAM got much better at a stream once it starts, and only a little better at the wait before it does. That is the setup for Post 35. Different metric, different physics (charge sensing, capacitor cells).
Parallelism to Hide a Slow Access# A channel is an independent controller path — concurrent requests need not queue behind each other. Within a channel, ranks and banks let one bank finish (or refresh — Post 10) while another takes a new request. Overlap enough independent accesses and aggregate throughput stays high even though no single access got faster. That is why the organization exists: not a catalog of DIMM features, a way to hide the latency the next post names as a wall.
A DIMM is the physical package — chips on a board with a standard edge connector — so capacity is “how many slots, what size,” not a redesign of the bus.
The next two posts are what happens when this negotiation falls short: the memory wall, and its cousin on the compute side, the clock-speed wall.

title: The Memory Wall
content:
Post 34 closed on a split: DDR bandwidth scaled; DRAM latency did not. Zoom out and that split is a system-level gap that has been widening for decades.
Diverging Exponentials# Wm. A. Wulf and Sally A. McKee named it in 1995. Processor speed and DRAM speed both improve exponentially, but the exponents differ — and the difference of diverging exponentials grows exponentially. CPU performance (Phase 3’s clocks and architecture) ran away; DRAM latency improved by a much smaller factor. They called the result the memory wall: not a nuisance better engineering quietly absorbs, a structural limit.
Why Bandwidth Moved and Latency Did Not# Not an oversight — physics. DRAM access latency is dominated by sensing a tiny charge on a capacitor (Post 10’s 1T1C cell) reliably enough to tell 1 from 0. That sensing does not scale down like transistor switching. Bandwidth can be raised without beating that limit: wider prefetch, more banks, more channels, double-data-rate transfer. Throughput without a shorter first access. That is why DDR generations (Post 34) sold bandwidth. Latency has stayed stubborn.
What the Gap Costs# A core waiting hundreds of cycles on one miss is not computing. The cache hierarchy (Post 15) is not a nicety; it is the industry’s main paper over the wall — keep the working set in SRAM so the CPU rarely pays full DRAM latency. Out-of-order execution (Post 16) hides some of the rest, overlapping independent work with a miss. Neither closes the gap. Both hide it for programs that are cache-friendly or have enough independent work.
Poor locality — large random structures, some graphs, some databases — still pays the wall in full. That is a large part of why bandwidth (not just capacity) became a first-class design target, and why GPU memory hierarchies and HBM (Phase 9) spend cost and complexity on moving bytes even though the first-bit wait barely budged. Next: a cousin wall, on the compute side, at almost the same historical moment.
Door out: Wm. A. Wulf and Sally A. McKee, “Hitting the Memory Wall: Implications of the Obvious” (ACM SIGARCH Computer Architecture News, 1995) — the short note that named the wall and showed why the gap would dominate unless something basic changed.

title: The Clock Speed Wall
content:
Post 35 was the memory-side wall: DRAM latency failing to keep up with the CPU. This is the compute-side wall that landed at almost the same moment. Together — not either one alone — they are why the industry pivoted to multicore (Post 17) and, later, to the fabrics in Post 37.
The Curve That Bent# Clock frequency climbed from the 1980s through the early 2000s, then flattened around 2004–2005. Desktop parts were near 4 GHz; with narrow exceptions, mainstream clocks stopped rising even as transistor counts (Moore’s Law, Phase 8) kept climbing. For decades those two had moved together. Then they did not.
P ≈ CV²f, and the Voltage Term# Dynamic power in CMOS is roughly capacitance × voltage squared × frequency. Frequency alone is linear in power — uncomfortable, not fatal. At a fixed process, a faster clock often needed a higher supply to stay reliable, and voltage is squared. Frequency and voltage rising together compound. The mid-2000s wall was also Dennard scaling breaking down and leakage limiting further voltage cuts. Heat, not a missed circuit trick.
A Thermal Ceiling, Same Kind as Skew# Power that becomes heat has to leave the die or the chip throttles (by design) or, worse, fails. By the mid-2000s, mainstream air cooling was already near its useful limit. Pushing clocks — and the voltage that came with them — further meant power densities that economical cooling could not remove. Same category as Post 32’s parallel-bus skew: a physical ceiling, not a design inefficiency you route around.
Wide Instead of Fast# Diminishing ILP (Post 17) and a hard power ceiling on one core: stop making one core faster; put several on the die, each at a more modest, more efficient clock. Aggregate throughput can still climb. No single core has to cross the thermal line that stopped frequency.
Two Walls, One Turn# The memory wall is DRAM latency losing to compute. The clock-speed wall is compute itself hitting heat. Different physics, same decade. Together they ended “make one core faster” as the growth story and forced “more cores — and, increasingly, move work onto specialized parallel hardware, then connect those units without going back through a general-purpose CPU.” That last clause is Post 37, and later GPUs (Phase 9) and accelerators (Phase 10).

title: Interconnects at Scale
content:
This phase so far connected parts inside one machine — CPU to memory, CPU to devices. Once a workload needs several GPUs, or several machines, the question changes: can those units talk to each other fast enough that the extra communication does not eat the extra compute?
The Default Path Is the Tax# Without a peer path, GPU A writes through system memory and GPU B reads it back — extra hops, extra latency, PCIe bandwidth spent on copies. Even on PCIe alone, GPUDirect P2P can DMA GPU↔GPU without host staging (still at PCIe rates). The remaining constraint is bandwidth and topology: a shared expansion fabric was never designed as a many-GPU mesh.
Dedicated Links, Coherent Memory, Fewer Copies# NVIDIA’s NVLink is a purpose-built GPU-to-GPU interconnect — CPU and system memory out of the transfer. An NVSwitch can make every GPU in a node reachable from every other, at bandwidth well above the PCIe-and-CPU path. For frequent, large exchanges — the pattern large-scale training returns to in Phases 7 and 10 — that direct path is first-order, not a tweak.
CXL (Compute Express Link) answers a neighboring constraint: cache-coherent access beyond one die, and, further out, pooled memory that is not soldered to a single socket. Capacity can move among compute nodes instead of being frozen to whichever DIMM slot it landed in — a flexibility neither DDR (Post 34) nor raw PCIe gives you.
GPUDirect RDMA lets a NIC read or write GPU memory directly. Without it, a GPU-to-GPU transfer across a network is GPU → system memory → NIC → far system memory → far GPU — copies that cost latency and memory bandwidth. Collapse that to GPU → network → GPU, for the same reason RDMA (Post 42) wins in storage and messaging: fewer copies, less CPU babysitting the move.
The Same Problem, Open Hardware# This is the conceptual base under the custom GPU memory fabric the series keeps pointing at: make remote GPU memory addressable without a general-purpose CPU in the path. NVLink and GPUDirect solve that inside one vendor’s stack. An open, PCIe-based alternative has to remove the same inefficiency — which is why Posts 32–33’s TLP-level peer path, and this post’s “why the dedicated link exists,” are the same story.

title: Serial Links and the First Machine-to-Machine Connections
content:
Every bus in Phase 5 stays inside one machine. Networking starts when separate machines must talk — and before packet-switched networks existed, that meant a serial link: one bit stream, point to point, no routing, no address beyond “the thing on the other end of this wire.”
RS-232: The Baseline Serial Link# RS-232 (EIA, 1960) fixed voltage levels and asynchronous serial conventions between two devices — both ends agree on baud rate in advance, because no clock rides with the data. No addressing, no routing, no error correction beyond whatever simple parity the ends chose. Just two devices, one bit at a time.
That was enough. Terminals used it to reach mainframes and minicomputers (Phase 3’s lineage). It is still the dead-simple console path into routers and embedded gear when you need a channel that does not depend on any higher networking stack.
The Modem: Digital Over Analog Wire# Long-haul talk had to ride the telephone network — analog, narrowband, built for voice. A modem modulates a digital bit stream onto an analog carrier the phone line can carry, and demodulates it back to bits at the far end. Early rates were hundreds of bits per second, later tens of kilobits — slow by modern measure, but the only practical way to reach a machine that was not in the same room, over infrastructure that already went nearly everywhere.
Why This Forces the Next Architecture# A point-to-point serial link — RS-232 direct or modem-over-phone — connects exactly two endpoints. There is no multi-node network and no routing decision for a destination that is not on the wire. Scaling to many machines that reach each other without a dedicated pair between every pair requires a different bet: break data into packets, route them hop by hop, share the links. That is what ARPANET set out to prove — next post.

title: ARPANET and Packet Switching
content:
Post 38’s serial links connect exactly two endpoints. ARPANET, live in 1969 under ARPA (later DARPA), set out to prove something else: many machines reaching many others without a dedicated circuit between every pair, by breaking data into packets routed independently hop by hop.
Circuit Switching vs Packet Switching# The telephone network Post 38 rode used circuit switching: reserve a continuous end-to-end path for the entire call, whether anyone is speaking or not. Fine for continuous voice; a poor fit for computer traffic, which is bursty — active transfer, then idle stretches during which a reserved circuit sits unused.
Packet switching takes the opposite bet. Break data into packets, each carrying a destination address; route each independently; share the physical links among many conversations. No path reserved for a whole session — packets from different transfers interleave, may take different routes, and reassemble at the destination. Paul Baran’s RAND work on distributed, survivable communications and Leonard Kleinrock’s queueing analysis of packet networks supplied the intellectual ground; Lawrence Roberts at ARPA turned the bet into a funded research network.
IMPs: The Original Routers# ARPANET’s hops were Interface Message Processors (IMPs) — dedicated minicomputers at each site (Phase 3’s minicomputer era, applied to the wire) that accepted packets from the local host, chose the next hop, and forwarded. Conceptually, that is what a modern router still does. The first four nodes — UCLA, Stanford Research Institute, UC Santa Barbara, University of Utah — were tiny by later standards. They were enough to show packet switching worked in practice, not only on paper.
Why This Was a Real Bet# Telecom engineers steeped in circuit switching often doubted a network without reserved paths could deliver data reliably at all. ARPANET’s success was institutional validation of an architecture that had real skepticism against it — not an inevitable “next step” everyone already agreed on.
What This Set Up# ARPANET’s own host-to-host protocols were not yet TCP/IP (Post 41). The architectural win — packets over dedicated circuits — is the foundation every later network in this phase builds on, through the modern internet, datacenter fabrics in Post 42, and Phase 10’s training-cluster interconnects. Next, local: how buildings standardized on Ethernet (Post 40) before TCP/IP tied heterogeneous nets into one internetwork.
Door out: Paul Baran, On Distributed Communications (RAND Corporation, 1964) — the classic distributed/packet argument that, with Kleinrock’s queueing work and Roberts’s ARPA program, underwrites why ARPANET could bet against circuit switching.

title: Ethernet and the Local Area Network
content:
ARPANET (Post 39) solved wide-area packet switching between distant sites. Inside one building, IMP-style routing for a few dozen meters of cable is the wrong tool. Ethernet, begun at Xerox PARC in 1973 by Robert Metcalfe and David Boggs, became the dominant local answer.
The Shared-Medium Problem# Early Ethernet put many stations on one shared cable — a bus topology, the same kind of contention Post 31 faced inside a machine, now on a LAN. Every station can transmit; every station hears every transmission. Two transmitters at once corrupt both.
CSMA/CD: Listen, Transmit, Detect, Back Off# Ethernet’s answer is CSMA/CD. Carrier Sense: listen first; transmit only if the medium looks idle. Multiple Access: any station may try — no central grant, unlike request/grant on system buses (Post 31). Collision Detection: keep listening while sending; if a collision appears, stop, wait a random backoff, retry.
Randomization is the load-bearing trick. Fixed identical backoffs would collide forever. Different random waits let one station succeed before the other retries — decentralized contention without an arbiter.
The Frame# Ethernet carries data in frames: source and destination MAC addresses (hardware addresses, below the IP addresses of Post 41), a type field for the higher protocol, payload, and a CRC — the same reliability kind as PCIe’s data-link checks (Post 33), on a different medium.
From Shared Bus to Switched Star# Modern wired Ethernet mostly left the shared cable for switches that give each station its own point-to-point link — the same shared-to-point-to-point escape PCIe made relative to older parallel buses (Post 32). On a proper switch, classic CSMA/CD collisions largely vanish: each link has two ends. The ideas still matter historically, and early Wi-Fi — still a shared radio medium — had to solve the same collision constraint.
Where This Leads# Local Ethernet plus wide-area packet routing still leave a gap: a universal addressing and routing scheme that ties different underlying technologies into one internetwork. That is TCP/IP — next.
Door out: Robert M. Metcalfe and David R. Boggs, “Ethernet: Distributed Packet Switching for Local Computer Networks” (Communications of the ACM, 1976) — the primary paper that stated the shared-medium LAN and CSMA/CD design.

title: TCP/IP and the Modern Internet Stack
content:
ARPANET (Post 39) proved packet switching. Ethernet (Post 40) standardized the local wire. Neither alone says how to stitch different networks — different media, different addressing — into one internetwork any two machines can use. Vint Cerf and Bob Kahn’s TCP/IP suite solved that; it is still the foundation the modern internet runs on.
The Layered Model# TCP/IP splits concerns the way PCIe’s stack does (Post 33), at internetworking scale. Link handles the local hop — Ethernet, Wi-Fi, fiber. Internet (IP) gives universal addressing and routing across those links; an IP packet does not care what medium carries it. Transport (TCP or UDP) offers either reliable ordered delivery (TCP) or minimal-overhead best-effort (UDP) on top of IP. Application is where HTTP, DNS, SMTP and kin sit, picking the transport that fits.
Encapsulation# Data moving down gains a header at each layer — application bytes under TCP/UDP, that segment under IP, that packet under a link header (and often trailer). At the far end the process reverses: each layer strips its header and uses what it just read (ports, addresses) to hand the remainder upward.
TCP on an Unreliable Substrate# IP is explicitly best-effort — no delivery promise, no ordering promise, drops allowed. TCP builds a reliable ordered byte stream on top with sequence numbers and acknowledgments (and retransmission when ACKs do not arrive) — the same reliability kind as PCIe’s data-link layer (Post 33), stretched across a whole unreliable internetwork instead of one dedicated link.
A connection starts with a three-way handshake: SYN (client proposes a sequence number), SYN-ACK (server acknowledges and proposes its own), final ACK. Only then does application data flow — a small deliberate cost so both sides share synchronized state first.
From One Network’s Protocols to a Stack# ARPANET originally spoke its own host-to-host protocol (NCP), not TCP/IP. Cerf and Kahn’s bet was larger: a protocol stack that could internet many packet networks, so the transport and the local wire could evolve separately. The practical cutover on the ARPANET itself was the January 1, 1983 “flag day,” when NCP was turned off and TCP/IP became mandatory — a rare hard cut that made the layered story operational, not only architectural.
Application protocols then stacked because that substrate existed. DNS (Post 64’s doors: RFC 1034 / RFC 1035) made names usable at scale; mail and the web (SMTP, HTTP and kin) rode TCP as clients of a reliable stream rather than reinventing addressing and retransmission. The pattern is the point: each layer buys one constraint so the layer above can assume it. That is a story about stacking, not a catalog of every RFC.
Why This Design Won# The load-bearing assumption was that the underlying network is heterogeneous and unreliable, so guarantees belong at a higher layer rather than in every physical link. That matched a global internetwork stitched over decades from different technologies by organizations that never agreed on one physical standard — which is why TCP/IP still sits under essentially the whole modern internet, including the datacenter networks next.
Door out: RFC 791 (Internet Protocol) and RFC 793 (Transmission Control Protocol) — the primary specs for the addressing/routing and reliable-transport halves of this stack (Cerf/Kahn lineage; Postel as RFC editor for these September 1981 texts).

title: Datacenter Networking and RDMA
content:
TCP/IP (Post 41) is the right backbone for a heterogeneous, unreliable, global network. Inside one datacenter — one owner, short distances, engineered fabric — that same kernel-mediated path starts to look like overhead for workloads that spend every microsecond and every byte of bandwidth.
Where the Overhead Comes From# A traditional TCP/IP send copies application data into a kernel buffer, runs the stack, and lets the NIC transmit — mirrored on receive. Each step costs CPU cycles and, worse for latency, real copies between memory locations. Fine for ordinary web traffic. Costly for HPC or distributed ML training that exchanges gradients many times per second.
RDMA: Kernel and CPU Off the Data Path# RDMA (Remote Direct Memory Access) lets one machine read or write another’s memory without the receiver’s CPU or kernel babysitting the transfer. The RDMA-capable adapter moves bytes memory-to-memory across the network. Same idea as GPUDirect RDMA in Post 37 — fewer copies, CPU freed for compute — applied between whole machines, not only between GPUs on a node.
Fat-Tree: Wiring Thousands Evenly# At thousands of machines, topology decides whether bandwidth is real or only advertised. A fat-tree structures switches so capacity scales predictably up the hierarchy instead of hiding bottleneck links that appear only under load. Large training clusters (Phase 10) are wired with that deliberation on purpose — not ad-hoc convenience.
Same Philosophy as This Series’s Fabric Work# Remove unnecessary copies; bypass the kernel where it is not needed; let hardware move data as directly as the topology allows. Post 37 applied that inside and across GPU nodes; this post applies it to machine-to-machine networking. Together they hand off to Phase 7’s distributed systems — starting with the pre-web internet’s own early find-and-talk systems.

title: Usenet, Archie, Gopher, and the Pre-Web Internet
content:
TCP/IP (Post 41) gave the internet a universal addressing and transport foundation. What ran on top of it, for roughly two decades before the World Wide Web became the dominant interface, was one arc with two faces: find something, then talk to someone. Distributed discussion, early search, menu-driven browsing, real-time chat, and finally consumer portals each solved a piece of that arc with the technology available at the time.
Usenet: Distributed Discussion, No Central Server# Usenet (Tom Truscott and Jim Ellis at Duke, conceived 1979, public 1980) predates the modern web by over a decade. No central server hosts all discussion. Participating servers exchange messages store-and-forward — first over UUCP dial-up, later over TCP/IP via NNTP (1986) — so a server receives posts from its peers, stores them, and forwards them on. A post propagates without a single central point of control.
Hierarchical newsgroups (comp.lang.c, rec.arts.movies, …) let discussion self-organize by topic without a central moderator imposing the tree. That design is a different philosophy from most of what replaced it — closer in spirit to distributed-systems ideas Post 44 covers, applied to human talk rather than data processing.
Archie: The First Search Tool# Before anything resembling a modern search engine, finding a specific file meant knowing which host held it. Archie (1990, McGill; Alan Emtage with Bill Heelan and Peter Deutsch) took a narrower cut: periodically poll known FTP servers, index public filenames, let users search the index. Contents were out of scope — only names — but that was still a large step past guessing the server.
Gopher: Menu-Driven Browsing Before the Web# Gopher (1991, University of Minnesota; Mark McCahill and colleagues) offered hierarchical, menu-driven navigation: documents, submenus, links to other Gopher servers, selected by number rather than free-form hyperlinks. More constrained than the web — and for a brief stretch in the early 1990s, a serious contender for how the internet’s information space would be organized.
IRC: Peer Talk in Real Time# Usenet was talk that propagated. IRC was talk that happened now. In August 1988, Jarkko Oikarinen at the University of Oulu built Internet Relay Chat to improve multi-user conversation on the OuluBox BBS — inspired in part by Bitnet Relay and local tools from Jyrki Kuoppala and Jukka Pihl — then watched servers link Finland to North America as friends ran ircd elsewhere. Channels, nicknames, and a federated mesh of servers gave the internet a live room without a single corporate host. The protocol later landed in RFC 1459 (Oikarinen and Darren Reed, 1993).
Door out: RFC 1459 — the primary IRC protocol specification.
Consumer Portals: Packaging Find and Talk# By the mid-1990s, the open tools above still assumed you knew where to point a client. Consumer portals sold a different bet: one homepage that bundled directory finding, news, mail, and chat so a newcomer did not have to assemble the arc themselves.
Yahoo is the seed of that kind. In 1994, Stanford graduate students Jerry Yang and David Filo started “Jerry and David’s Guide to the World Wide Web” — a human-curated hierarchical directory — renamed it Yahoo!, and grew it into a portal that layered search, mail, and other sticky services on top of the directory. Derive the kin and stop: AOL’s walled garden, Excite, Lycos, and similar front doors were the same category — attention hubs that packaged find-then-talk for a mass audience — not a second company encyclopedia. Door out: treat the portal era as product history sitting on the protocols above, not as a replacement for them.
Why the Open Web Outran the Menus and the Hubs# The web’s core move — HTML with hyperlinks that could point to any other document, anywhere, not locked to a fixed menu hierarchy or one portal’s taxonomy — was a more flexible find model than Gopher menus or a curated directory. Netscape Navigator (1994), from a company founded by former NCSA Mosaic developers with commercial backing and fast iteration, pushed that model from research tool into mainstream use. Portals kept packaging the arc; the open hyperlink graph (and later, crawler-scale search in the next post) kept winning the find half.
Gopher faded from mainstream use. Usenet and IRC never fully disappeared — they just stopped being most people’s first door. Archie’s filename index was a seed of a kind that Post 44 scales into indexing a whole decentralized web.
Why This Belongs in This Series# Find and talk are not side trivia. Usenet’s decentralized propagation, Archie’s index-over-distributed-hosts problem, IRC’s federated live rooms, and the portal bet to productize all of it resurface as the same category of questions the next posts ask at larger scale: how do you search a space with no central catalog, and how do people stay in conversation once the wire is shared?
